summary: Classify a string as a valid IPv4, valid IPv6 or neither.
mainInsight: Split by '.' (4 parts) or ':' (8 parts) and validate each part: IPv4 parts are 1-3 digits, no leading zeros (except '0'), value 0..255; IPv6 parts are 1-4 hexadecimal digits (leading zeros allowed, case-insensitive). Reject empty parts and other characters.

approaches.name: Split and validate parts
approaches.summary: Check the separator, count and each part.

commonMistakes: Accepting values above 255 or hex digits in IPv4

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Split on the separator and validate each part against its format rules. Clue: The statement defines both formats part by part (four decimal parts up to 255 without leading zeros, eight hex parts of up to four digits), so split and check each part.
keyPoints: The statement defines both formats part by part (four decimal parts up to 255 without leading zeros, eight hex parts of up to four digits), so split and check each part.
cards.explanation: The formats are fully specified, so a split plus per-part checks decides the answer.

promptVariants: How do the validity rules differ between IPv4 and IPv6 parts?
options: IPv4: no leading zeros, 0..255; IPv6: 1-4 hex digits (zeros ok)
IPv4 allows hex digits; IPv6 allows only decimal digits
Both need exactly the same number of digits in each part
IPv6 forbids leading zeros; IPv4 allows them in a part
cards.answer: IPv4: no leading zeros, 0..255; IPv6: 1-4 hex digits (zeros ok)
cards.explanation: '01' is invalid in IPv4, '0001' is valid in IPv6.

incorrectOptionExplanations.IPv4 allows hex digits; IPv6 allows only: It is the other way round.

promptVariants: Which empty or malformed inputs must be rejected?
How do you handle a trailing separator?
cards.answer: A trailing or leading separator creates an empty part when split, and an empty part is invalid. Split with an explicit separator (not split() with no argument), count exactly 4 or 8 parts, and reject any part with non-allowed characters.
cards.explanation: Python's str.isdigit also accepts some Unicode digits; check with an ASCII set.
